strategy.headline: Oklahoma has one big-league team. Dress the whole state in Thunder blue, under $100.
strategy.thesis: Apart from the Hornets' 2005-07 Katrina stay, the Thunder are the only big-league team Oklahoma has ever had. The market is the whole state: Tulsa, Norman, Lawton, Stillwater, tribal nations and small-town gyms. In a house split between Sooners and Cowboys, Thunder blue is the one color everyone shares, so every piece starts blue, the City Edition included. Fans are proud of a 2025 title and a roster Sam Presti drafted and developed, led by back-to-back MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. A seven-game West finals loss to San Antonio still stings. Win with a deep 'Oklahoma' layer under $100 in big-box and mall doors statewide. Add a few credited, paid artist drops from the Plaza, Paseo, Deep Deuce and Tulsa, and a blue-bodied 2027-28 City Edition with 'Oklahoma' across the chest.

archetype.name: The One-Team State
archetype.description: A whole state that adopted a franchise in 2008 and now wears a champion as its civic uniform. Loud, loyal, value-minded and allergic to flash the team has not earned.

pulse.teamMoment: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is a back-to-back MVP, and his Thunder went 64-18 before San Antonio beat them 4-3 in the West finals. They're 2026-27 co-title favorites, with a BetMGM win total of 60.5, the West's highest. Luguentz Dort went to Atlanta, and Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins were traded too. In came draft picks Aday Mara (No. 12), Bennett Stirtz and Otega Oweh. Presti is keeping a payroll near $260M rather than cutting it.
pulse.sentiment: Confident but stung. Fans expect a title and see the Oct 20 opener at San Antonio as a grudge match. They trust Presti and Mark Daigneault's patient build, even as familiar rotation players leave.

topInsights.title: The market is Oklahoma, not OKC
topInsights.insight: There's no NFL, MLB or NHL team in the state. Thunder fans drive in from Tulsa, Lawton, Norman and Stillwater, and they shop big-box and mall doors along I-35, I-40 and the Turner Turnpike. The state outline and the word 'Oklahoma' travel everywhere. Area codes don't: 405 is the OKC metro, 918 is Tulsa, and 580 covers the west and south.
topInsights.implication: Lead the statewide line with the state outline and an 'Oklahoma' wordmark. Sell 405, 918 and 580 as a matched area-code set, aimed door by door. Give Tulsa (Utica Square, Woodland Hills) its own allocation.

topInsights.title: Thunder blue keeps the peace in a Sooner-and-Cowboy house
topInsights.insight: Fall closets run OU crimson and OSU orange, plenty of households are split, and everyone is Thunder. Orange-heavy or crimson-leaning blocking reads as a college pick. A burnt-orange body reads as Texas.
topInsights.implication: Make every Thunder piece blue-bodied, the City Edition included, with Sunset (#EF3B24) and red-clay rust as trim. Launch midweek or on Thunder Cup Fridays, never on football Saturdays.

topInsights.title: Red Dirt is a Stillwater sound and a Stockyards wardrobe
topInsights.insight: Red Dirt music grew out of Stillwater's songwriter scene, and Turnpike Troubadours and John Moreland carry it now. Its look lives on gig posters for rooms like Tulsa's Cain's Ballroom and in Stockyards City stores like Langston's. The clay itself stains every sneaker in the state.
topInsights.implication: Make a rust (#A8442A) and canvas capsule with gig-poster lettering by a commissioned Oklahoma poster artist. Launch it at a show booked by a Red Dirt venue. Always sell it next to a hoops-first blue line, so the Thunder never read as a country brand.

topInsights.title: Own the sky through Oklahoma landmarks, not gradients
topInsights.insight: Storm fronts and sunsets are real here, but a sky gradient alone could be Kansas City or Denver. The Thunder palette is already a sunset. Only Oklahoma has the Skydance Bridge's scissortail sail over I-40, the Deco rooflines of downtown Tulsa and OKC, and the flat sky-blue field of the state flag.
topInsights.implication: Make the Skydance sail line and stepped Deco silhouettes the signature graphics. Keep packable shells core from October to April. Hold any gradient headline until the earlier City Editions are checked, and never use tornado-damage or memorial imagery.

topInsights.title: Homegrown pride, Gilgeous-Alexander style
topInsights.insight: Fans are proudest of a core Presti drafted and developed (Williams, Holmgren, now Mara) and of Loud City at Paycom Center. They don't want a victory lap. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, from Hamilton, Ontario, is one of the league's most-watched tunnel dressers, with a Canadian following of his own.
topInsights.implication: Write opener and season copy about development and Loud City, not revenge for a loss. Keep any 2025 champion reference to licensed marks. Add a Gilgeous-Alexander tunnel-fit story once the brand and licensing path for his product is confirmed.

topInsights.title: Value-minded ritual buyers with a hard $100 line
topInsights.insight: Oklahomans buy in person: Penn Square, Academy, Dick's, Hibbett, the arena store and the Nike Factory Store at OKC Outlets on I-40. An August sales-tax holiday on clothing and shoes under $100 lands on school start. Nike has no community or flagship door in town.
topInsights.implication: Price a full Thunder ladder of tees, shorts, hoodies and youth footwear at $99 or less, with deep youth sizes. Tell the story in borrowed venues: the arena, Plaza and Midtown pop-ups, local gyms.

topInsights.title: The richest stories belong to specific communities
topInsights.insight: The state's deepest design sources are its communities. They include dozens of sovereign Native nations, Deep Deuce jazz and Clara Luper's 1958 sit-ins, and Tulsa's Greenwood and Black Wall Street. There's also the Classen Asian District, Southside car culture and the NW 39th Gayborhood. None of them is a theme to borrow, and even a name like 'Red Earth' already belongs to a Native institution.
topInsights.implication: Any piece drawing on these communities starts with a named partner. The partner sets terms, approves the work, is credited and paid, and launches it at a community event. No regalia, sacred imagery, scripts or memorial imagery.

scorecard.rationale: The league's second-most intense fandom and a 60.5-win co-favorite with a Converse-signed star put opportunity in the top ten (scored on demand and Nike's rights position, not doors), while small-metro, value-minded retail and a thinner design well than the culture capitals keep retail and culture below average (brief scores: opportunity 70, culture 66, retail 40, fandom 86). music.headline: Oklahoma City sounds like storytellers and prairie sky, not Nashville gloss
music.summary: Oklahoma music is songwriter-first: Woody Guthrie, Bob Wills' Western swing, the Tulsa Sound of J.J. Cale and Leon Russell, and Stillwater's Red Dirt. OKC adds The Flaming Lips, Jabee's hip-hop on the Northeast side and Native artists such as Samantha Crain. Music meets the Thunder mostly at the arena, not through one signature anthem. The way in is design: gig posters and prairie sky, with Red Dirt as the credibility test.

insights.title: Red Dirt is the local genre, not generic country
insights.detail: Red Dirt grew out of Stillwater's bar rooms in the 1970s-90s (Bob Childers, Jimmy LaFave, Cross Canadian Ragweed). Turnpike Troubadours, John Moreland and Parker Millsap carry it today. Fans hear it as songwriter music that is proudly not Nashville.
insights.implication: Go earthy, worn and honest, with plain type and no rhinestone-country cliches. A Red Dirt-coded capsule tells insiders you did the homework.

insights.title: Folk protest and dance-hall swing are the roots
insights.detail: Guthrie is from Okemah, and the Woody Guthrie Folk Festival there each July is a pilgrimage. Bob Wills' Western swing is the Tulsa-rooted dance-hall ancestor. The Dust Bowl story is about endurance, which echoes the Thunder's 2025 title run.
insights.implication: Tell a story about endurance and wind, not cowboy kitsch. Credit the Guthrie estate, and don't lift his guitar-slogan imagery without a license.

insights.title: The Flaming Lips make weird a point of civic pride
insights.detail: The Flaming Lips are from OKC, and Wayne Coyne is a local fixture. Bubble Tour-style spectacle, confetti and animal costumes define the city's quirkier side, and the Plaza District and Automobile Alley carry that arts energy.
insights.implication: Offer a playful, psychedelic gradient or graphic as a limited drop beyond Thunder blue and orange. Any Lips artwork or name needs a license.

insights.title: Deep Deuce jazz to Northeast hip-hop and R&B

art.headline: OKC looks like red dirt, Route 66 neon and Plains Deco, under the Thunder's sunset
art.summary: Oklahoma City's art lives in small, fiercely local districts, not on one famous mural wall. The street look is mid-century roadside: Route 66 neon, hand-painted brick signs, Art Deco. The Thunder's blue, sunset orange and yellow already work as the civic palette. Lead with local makers and with Native and Black Oklahoma artists, and skip the Land Run and Western cliches.

insights.title: The districts are the scene
insights.detail: The Plaza District is on NW 16th, anchored by the Plaza District Association and its mural program and festivals. The Paseo Arts District has Spanish Pueblo Revival bungalows and working studios. Automobile Alley has its own look too. Locals identify with a district more than with a citywide art brand.
insights.implication: Brief a district-by-district capsule or collab series (Plaza, Paseo, Deep Deuce) instead of one generic OKC graphic. District names work as small-run graphic titles.

insights.title: Red clay below, flag blue above
insights.detail: Oklahoma clay reads as a deep oxide red, and the state flag's field is a flat sky blue. With the Thunder's blue and sunset orange, they sit very close to the team's own palette. Red dirt also names a whole local music and apparel idiom.
insights.implication: A red-clay colorway (washed, garment-dyed look) next to Thunder blue is a premium alternative to the default blue and orange, and it stays true to the place.

insights.title: Route 66 neon and Deco set the type
insights.detail: The city remembers its signs. Neon runs down Route 66 (Pops on the Arcadia stretch, with its giant soda-bottle sign, plus motel and diner script). Automobile Alley has showroom lettering. Art Deco and Streamline Moderne buildings mark downtown and Tulsa (Boston Avenue Methodist Church, Philtower). Hand-painted ghost signs and brick wall lettering are common in Bricktown and the Plaza.
insights.implication: Use script-and-block neon lettering, outlined slab type and stepped Deco geometry for graphics and jersey numbers. Tie it to the Route 66 centennial (2026) only after licensing is checked.

insights.title: Native design: the strongest source, the highest risk
insights.detail: Oklahoma's 39 tribal nations are the state's deepest design heritage: Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee, Osage, Kiowa, Comanche and many more. Living artists include Yatika Starr Fields (Cherokee/Osage/Muscogee, a muralist and painter based in Tulsa). The Red Earth Festival in Oklahoma City is a long-standing venue for Native artists, and the state flag is built on an Osage battle shield.
insights.implication: Pay and credit a Native artist or nation-approved partner for a real collaboration. Don't lift regalia, ceremonial patterns or tribal symbols as decoration, and keep Native work out of team-branded graphics without that partnership.

insights.title: Black Oklahoma artists own the Deep Deuce story
insights.detail: Deep Deuce (Deep Second) was the Black jazz and business district that shaped Charlie Christian and Ralph Ellison. Northeast OKC and Tulsa's Greenwood district carry mural and memorial work around Black Wall Street. These stories are tied to real loss and recovery, and local Black artists, not outside brands, own the narrative.
insights.implication: If you use it, start with community partners and make Black Oklahoma artists the lead creators, with revenue share. Greenwood and the 1921 massacre are not a decorative theme.

insights.title: Thunder iconography is already the shared civic art
insights.detail: Thunder blue, sunset orange and yellow, the thunderbolt-and-basketball marks and the Loud City crowd culture are painted on walls, murals and shop fronts across the metro. Thunder fan art and local print makers sell heavily through gig posters, Plaza shops and fan markets.
insights.implication: Frame local artist collabs on official product as a flip on Thunder colors, not a competing identity. Let artists reinterpret the team's sunset and storm sky.

food.headline: OKC eats like a Southern Plains crossroads, and the onion burger is the dish to own
food.summary: Oklahoma eats stockyard beef, fried-and-smothered comfort food and the onion burger, a Depression-era thrift dish. Real immigrant corridors run alongside, chiefly Classen's Asian District and South OKC's Latino scene, and Lao and Native chefs lead a newer wave. The food brands locals wear are Braum's, Cattlemen's and Route 66 diners, not trendy newcomers. For a small-market-proud, two-time-contending team, food merch should stay modest and local. Written from model knowledge, so check each spot is still open.

insights.title: El Reno's onion burger is Oklahoma's own
insights.detail: Thin patties pressed into a heap of griddled onions are the El Reno original (Sid's Diner, Hamburger Inn). In OKC, Nic's Grill and Tucker's Onion Burgers carry it on. El Reno holds a Fried Onion Burger Day each spring. The dish is thrift-born, working-class and Oklahoma-specific.
insights.implication: Borrow the onion burger's look: translucent caramel onion, griddle sear, wax-paper wrap. Use it as a graphic and colorway story, not a literal burger icon. It passes the swap test.

insights.title: Stockyards beef is the origin myth
insights.detail: Cattlemen's Steakhouse sits in Stockyards City, beside the Oklahoma National Stockyards. It has served ranchers, politicians and ballplayers since the 1910s, and it's known for red-and-white neon and a breakfast of lamb fries and brains-and-eggs lore. It ties OKC's cowboy identity to the Thunder's blue-collar self-image.
insights.implication: Western-work textures (saddle leather, wool blanket stripes, cattle-brand marks) can give a Statement or lifestyle drop an OKC-only food-and-ranch anchor.

insights.title: Classen's Asian District is the corridor insiders mean
insights.detail: The Asian District runs along N. Classen Blvd, roughly NW 23rd to 30th. It grew from the Vietnamese community after 1975 and is anchored by Super Cao Nguyen market and a dense run of pho, banh mi and Chinese-Vietnamese spots. It hosts the Lunar New Year Festival and Asian night-market style events. Chef Jeff Chanchaleune opened Ma Der Lao Kitchen in the Plaza District in 2021, with sister noodle bar Bar Sen. It has made Lao food a nationally recognized OKC story.
insights.implication: Partner with Vietnamese and Lao creators and business owners, and pay them, for any graphic work. Never lift script or temple imagery as decoration.

insights.title: Native foodways are Oklahoma's deepest, least-merchandised layer
insights.detail: Oklahoma is home to 39 tribal nations. Indian tacos on frybread, Three Sisters crops and wild onions are living cuisine at powwows, the OKC Red Earth Festival and the Oklahoma City Native community. Potawatomi chef Loretta Barrett Oden is a pioneering voice in Native American food.
insights.implication: Reference Native food only through a tribal-artist partnership, with credit and compensation. Avoid ceremonial or regalia imagery entirely.

insights.title: Braum's is the dairy brand everyone wears
insights.detail: Oklahoma-born Braum's ice cream stores and fresh markets mark the state's identity, with a red-and-white look and loyalty that makes the logo a nostalgic wearable. Ice cream after a win is a common family ritual.
insights.implication: Braum's is third-party IP. Get a license, or nod to it only through generic dairy cues (cone-pink, soft-serve swirl) in lifestyle graphics.

insights.title: Game-day food is Bricktown-to-Midtown and very drive-in
insights.detail: Fans pregame around Bricktown, Midtown and Deep Deuce before Paycom Center, then scatter to watch parties at neighborhood bars and homes. The Thunder's 2025 title turned the whole metro into a watch-party town. The culture is casual and family-forward, with fried chicken, brisket and queso more common than fine dining.
insights.implication: Run pop-up giveaways at Bricktown and Midtown restaurants and watch-party partners, not only at the arena.

culture.headline: Oklahoma City spent a century as flyover country. Now it has the NBA's best team.
culture.summary: OKC runs on a chip on its shoulder. The prairie capital was founded in an afternoon, known nationally for the 1995 bombing and its tornadoes, and rebuilt through MAPS civic projects. The Thunder, in from Seattle in 2008, made it feel big-league. Now it has a back-to-back MVP in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and a fresh seven-game West finals loss to San Antonio. The mood is hungry, not entitled.

insights.title: Seattle origin story is a point of pride
insights.detail: The Thunder came from Seattle in 2008. Locals tell it as a town that earned a team by hosting the Hornets after Katrina and was ready when the chance came. Fans cite the Thunder first as proof the city belongs among big-league markets.
insights.implication: Lead with OKC-owned symbols, not generic Thunder branding. The city and state are the story, so the product should read as homegrown, not relocated.

insights.title: Resilience is the civic religion
insights.detail: The 1995 federal building bombing, the repeated May tornado outbreaks and the Oklahoma Standard of neighbors helping neighbors define how locals see themselves. Pride here is communal, not flashy. The Oklahoma City National Memorial is sacred ground, not a tourist backdrop.
insights.implication: Use storm-sky and sunrise language for toughness and togetherness. Never put tragedy imagery, the memorial's chairs or tornado destruction on product.

insights.title: The state's name is Choctaw
insights.detail: Oklahoma's name is Choctaw in origin, and the state is home to dozens of tribal nations, including the Chickasaw, Choctaw, Cherokee, Muscogee and Seminole. The First Americans Museum in OKC, opened in 2021, is the main civic institution telling that story.
insights.implication: Native-informed design must come from a tribal artist or nation through a paid partnership. No ceremonial or sacred imagery, and no mascot-style use.

insights.title: Northeast OKC holds the Black heritage
insights.detail: Deep Deuce was the hub of Black jazz and commerce: the Oklahoma City Blue Devils, Charlie Christian, Jimmy Rushing and the roots of Ralph Ellison. Clara Luper led the 1958 lunch-counter sit-ins. Northeast OKC remains the heart of that heritage.
insights.implication: A jazz-era type and Luper-inspired story collection works only with local Black creators and historians credited and paid, and tied to community reinvestment.

insights.title: 405 against 918: two Oklahomas, one outline
insights.detail: 405 is the metro's shorthand, and the state outline, panhandle included, is everywhere as a local graphic. Tulsa (918) is the in-state rival, with its own Greenwood District history. Sooners versus Cowboys loyalty runs through every family.
insights.implication: State-shape and 405 graphics travel across the whole fanbase. Mind the Tulsa and college rivalries so a Thunder product doesn't alienate half the state.

insights.title: Wind and big sky shape dress and mood

underground.headline: OKC's underground wears work boots and remixes its Thunder gear
underground.summary: Oklahoma City's scenes are small enough to overlap. The same people show up at a Plaza District art night, a Tower Theatre or Diamond Ballroom show, and a Paycom Center game. Under Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, team gear has become a civic uniform that the scenes customize. Nike earns its place here with craft, durability and local credit, not manufactured hype.

insights.title: Western wear is the local streetwear base layer
insights.detail: Stockyards City keeps pearl snaps, boot-cut denim, felt hats and tooled leather in everyday circulation. It's home to long-running outfitters like Langston's Western Wear and to the Oklahoma National Stockyards. Young locals pair the look with Thunder jerseys and Jordan or Nike retros. Rodeo and ranch dress is worn without irony here, unlike coastal western trend cycles.
insights.implication: Build Thunder product that sits next to boots and denim: heavy canvas, snap-button details, tooled-leather-texture graphics. Treat it as work-and-ranch heritage, not costume.

insights.title: Respect the Southside lowriders and trucks
insights.detail: OKC's Latino communities, centered on the Southside and Capitol Hill corridor, keep up lowrider, custom truck and quinceanera-car traditions: club plaques, candy paint, pinstriping. Cruising and shows are family events, not sideshows.
insights.implication: Candy-paint gradients, pinstripe line work and club-plaque badging can inform a capsule. Work only through paid collaboration with local clubs and painters.

insights.title: Plaza District and Paseo drive the DIY art scene
insights.detail: The Plaza District's annual Plaza Walls mural festival and the Paseo Arts District's First Friday gallery walks draw young crowds. Muralists, zine makers, screen printers and vinyl-sticker artists work the room. Factory Obscura, an OKC-based immersive art collective, and the Flaming Lips orbit give the state a weird-and-proud streak. That orbit runs on Wayne Coyne's psychedelic, DIY aesthetic.
insights.implication: Commission local muralists and screen printers for limited tees and hangtags. Psychedelic color pops against the Thunder's blue-and-sunset palette make a credible, non-corporate drop.

insights.title: Queer nightlife is concentrated and community-run
insights.detail: The NW 39th Street Gayborhood anchors OKC's LGBTQ+ nightlife, drag and Pride, with Oklahoma City Pride in June. Visibility carries real political stakes in this state. Nightlife crews there prize bold, glam, customized looks.
insights.implication: Partner with venues and organizers, with visible funding, and skip the rainbow-washing. Make any Pride-month moment a donation, co-credited. Don't print a slogan tee.

insights.title: Thunder gear gets customized, not just bought
insights.detail: Since the 2025 title and Gilgeous-Alexander's back-to-back MVPs, local fans screen print, embroider and thrift-flip Thunder pieces. Sunset orange and electric blue now read as OKC colors, not just team colors. Thrift and vintage buyers hunt Seattle SuperSonics-era and 2008-09 first-season Thunder gear.
insights.implication: Make repairable, remixable product: blank panels, patch-ready jackets and tees. A thrift-style vintage-wash line honors the early Thunder years.

insights.title: Native Oklahoma sets the terms
insights.detail: Oklahoma is home to 39 tribal nations. Events like the Red Earth Festival in OKC and the Native-led art in the Plaza and Paseo are community, not aesthetics. The Thunder and the Paycom Center area sit within this living history.
insights.implication: Don't lift regalia, beadwork patterns or sacred imagery. If you engage, work only through tribal-nation or Native-artist-led partnerships, with pay, credit and approval.

hoops.headline: Oklahoma basketball lives in high school gyms, and it was there before the Thunder
hoops.summary: Oklahoma basketball predates the Thunder. Black hoops pride runs through Tulsa's Booker T. Washington and OKC's Douglass. Native nations run their own gym-and-tournament circuits, and college loyalty splits four ways. The Thunder arrived in 2008 with no pro team ahead of them, so the whole state claims them. Meet that state in its gyms and high school stands, not only at Paycom Center.

insights.title: Fans drive in from Tulsa, Lawton and Norman
insights.detail: Apart from the Hornets' temporary 2005-07 stay after Katrina, the Thunder (2008) are the only major pro team Oklahoma has had, and in 2025 they gave the state a champion. Fans from Tulsa, Lawton, Norman and small-town gyms drive in for games. Rural and tribal communities claim the team as much as metro OKC does.
insights.implication: Plan events statewide, with Tulsa and Norman as real second and third hubs, not just Bricktown and Paycom Center.

insights.title: College loyalties run deeper than team colors
insights.detail: Sooners (now in the SEC), Cowboys, Tulsa and Oral Roberts each have loyal followings, and Thunder players with local college ties get claimed twice. Families often split blue-and-orange between Thunder and OSU.
insights.implication: Avoid orange-heavy and crimson-heavy product that reads as a college allegiance by accident. Anchor Thunder product in Thunder blue, sunset orange and yellow.

insights.title: High school hoops is community glue
insights.detail: Programs like Booker T. Washington in Tulsa, Douglass and Millwood in OKC, Edmond Santa Fe and Heritage Hall carry neighborhood pride. In March, the state tournaments fill arenas with whole towns.
insights.implication: School-spirit team sets and warm-ups for Oklahoma high school programs could quietly build credibility.

insights.title: Native basketball is a living tradition
insights.detail: Oklahoma is home to 39 tribal nations. School and community gyms in Native communities run their own tournaments and rivalries. Native players and families form a large and loyal Thunder base.
insights.implication: On any collaboration, work with Native designers and community organizations, credited and paid. Never lift ceremonial or sacred imagery.

insights.title: Development culture, not star-chasing
insights.detail: Under Sam Presti, the Thunder's identity is patient player development, with the OKC Blue as the G League feeder. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, the back-to-back MVP, is its face. Fans take pride in drafted and developed players like Chet Holmgren, Jalen Williams and now Aday Mara.
insights.implication: Tell worker-bee, earned-not-given stories in campaigns. This market is allergic to flash that isn't backed by work.

insights.title: Gilgeous-Alexander bridges Hamilton and OKC
insights.detail: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is a Hamilton, Ontario native and back-to-back MVP. OKC embraces him as its own, as it did Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook in earlier eras. His sneaker and style choices lead local trends.
insights.implication: Signature and team-adjacent product tied to Gilgeous-Alexander is the strongest single hook in the market.

fanbase.headline: Thunder fans wear the team's blue before any player's name
fanbase.summary: The Thunder carry a whole state, from Deep Deuce to Tulsa to rural towns that drive hours to Paycom Center. Fans take pride in noise, civility and loyalty. Heading into 2026-27 the mood is confident with an edge, tempered by the 4-3 loss to San Antonio that ended the title defense.

insights.title: No NFL, MLB or NHL, just the Thunder
insights.detail: With no NFL, MLB or NHL franchise, the Thunder are the shared identity of Oklahoma City, Tulsa and the small towns between. College football splits the state only on Saturdays, between Sooners and Cowboys.
insights.implication: Treat Oklahoma, not just OKC, as the market. Use state-shaped graphics, and take retail and drops to Tulsa and rural fans, not just Bricktown.

insights.title: Blue is the identity, not a player
insights.detail: Gameday crowds are a wall of Thunder blue, in team-issued shirts and blue-out nights, not a sea of star jerseys. Gilgeous-Alexander jerseys are now the clear top seller.
insights.implication: Lead with team-color Icon and Statement pieces and tonal blue basics. Add Gilgeous-Alexander as the featured player layer, not the only story.

insights.title: Seattle history is a sensitive subtext
insights.detail: The franchise arrived from Seattle in 2008. OKC fans claim the whole Durant-Westbrook-Harden era, the 2012 Finals loss and the 2025 banner as theirs. Sonics heritage belongs to Seattle fans, and the team handles it with care.
insights.implication: Keep Sonics green and gold and Seattle references out of OKC product. Stick to Oklahoma-era moments.

insights.title: Champions with unfinished business
insights.detail: The 2025 title is fresh pride. But San Antonio ended the title defense with a 4-3 West finals win in 2026, so the October 20 opener there is a redemption game.
insights.implication: Build the campaign copy and drops on unfinished business. Opening night is the emotional hook.

insights.title: A young core fans feel they raised
insights.detail: Fans watched Williams, Holmgren and now Mara and the 2026 draft class get drafted and developed. That builds patient trust in Sam Presti and Mark Daigneault, even as payroll climbs toward roughly $260M.
insights.implication: Make player-pairing content and youth-scale product for the next wave of fans. Talk about development and craft, not hype.

insights.title: Weather and sky as local language
insights.detail: Thunder, storms, wind and the big prairie sky are everyday Oklahoma, and they are the brand's visual DNA, from the sunset-orange accent to Thunder Up.
insights.implication: Sky, storm-front and sunset gradients feel native here. Use them for graphics and colorways.

rhythm.headline: The Thunder year starts high in October and peaks in April and May
rhythm.summary: The Thunder are the only major-league team in the state, so the whole state shows up, in the arena and in retail data. Football, storm season and the Women's College World Series shape the calendar around the playoffs. This year's title co-favorite opens at San Antonio, where its West finals run ended. Demand clusters around opening night, Christmas, the playoff run and the days after a series win.

insights.title: Watch parties run far from Bricktown
insights.detail: With no NFL, MLB or NHL team in the state, the Thunder carry Oklahoma's whole pro-sports identity. Fans drive in from Tulsa, Lawton, Norman and Stillwater, and watch parties run far from Bricktown.
insights.implication: Plan drops and pop-ups beyond OKC: Tulsa, Norman, Stillwater and the tribal casino-resort markets. Ship product as "Oklahoma" as well as "OKC".

insights.title: Football owns the fall, and fans wear both
insights.detail: October and November belong to OU and OSU football (crimson/cream and orange). The Oct 20 opener and the Friday Cup games land mid-week or on Friday nights, so attention is shared. Many households split between Sooners and Cowboys, but all of them are Thunder.
insights.implication: Stay out of the Saturday football window. Make Thunder blue the shared color, and skip crimson or orange blocking that reads as a college rival.

insights.title: Spring playoffs are the civic peak
insights.detail: In the playoff months the city turns out in blue for "Loud City" games, with watch parties at the Paycom Center plaza and in Bricktown. After a West finals loss, fans expect a deep run, and a series win changes retail demand within 24 hours.
insights.implication: Hold inventory and graphics capacity for a fast-turn playoff drop from mid-April: T-shirts, hoodies and series-specific pieces. Anchor everything in Thunder blue and sunset orange. Fans buy proof of belonging.

insights.title: Weather sets the apparel calendar
insights.detail: Oklahoma summers are hot and long, and spring brings severe weather. Fall and winter are short and variable, with cold snaps and ice storms. Spring tornado watches change game-night routines: the arena has policies, and fans watch with weather alerts on.
insights.implication: Layer up from October to April with hoodies, warm-ups and lightweight windbreakers. Cover the June to September gap with breathable tees. A wind- and storm-ready outer layer fits the state's identity.

insights.title: The Cup matters more than Christmas
insights.detail: The Dec 25 game is at Minnesota (8:00 p.m. ET). There's no home Christmas party, but it's a national-TV moment and a gift-buying peak. The NBA Cup Friday games (West Group B with MIN, LAC, NOP, MEM) turn November into a mini-playoff for OKC fans. In December the Cup knockout can bring a home semifinal if OKC is the higher seed.
insights.implication: Treat Black Friday to Dec 25 as the biggest gift window. Build court-inspired Cup pieces for group play. Holiday giving skews to jerseys, hoodies and youth sizes.

insights.title: Offseason is quiet, but the draft is real
insights.detail: July to September drops sharply. The exceptions are Summer League, the state fair in September and football kickoff. The Thunder's draft capital makes late June a lively window for fan talk, and Presti's moves get discussed like a civic project.
insights.implication: Use the quiet months for launches aimed at long-lead buyers (youth, collectors), city-specific graphics and a City Edition reveal buildup. Skip the hard sell.

uniform.headline: The Thunder look is clean and loved. The open ground is Oklahoma itself.
uniform.summary: OKC's core palette is Thunder Blue, Sunset, Yellow and Dark Blue. It's young, and now that the team is a champion, fans guard it as sacred. The City Edition line has been patchy: the 2025-26 set recolored a 2018-19 design. That leaves room for a ground-up Oklahoma story drawn from Deep Deuce jazz, Clara Luper's 1958 sit-ins, Route 66 and, only through partnership, Native nations.

insights.title: A young palette fans now protect
insights.detail: The Thunder's blue, sunset orange-red and yellow date from the 2008 relaunch. A whole generation of OKC fans grew up with exactly this set and treats it as theirs. Departures that ignore it tend to read as off-brand.
insights.implication: Build City and lifestyle work as extensions of Sunset and Yellow, with gradients and tonal blues, not new primary colors.

insights.title: City Edition: weakest chapter, biggest opening
insights.detail: The 2025-26 City Edition was a recolored 2018-19 set, an admission that the line has lacked a single defining Oklahoma concept. OKC has no City Edition to match the cult favorites in other markets.
insights.implication: Make a 2027-28 City Edition with an original, locally co-authored story. It could become the first OKC jersey fans collect, not just wear.

insights.title: Gold and banner details now mean a title
insights.detail: The Thunder won the 2025 title, then lost the 2026 West finals to San Antonio in seven. The mood is hungry. Fans want proof of the title run without the gloating.
insights.implication: Make champion-patch, banner and "Loud City" graphics read as earned and defiant. Pair them with Gilgeous-Alexander and Holmgren player-led drops.

insights.title: The Seattle origin is a quiet, unresolved layer
insights.detail: The franchise moved from Seattle in 2008, and the green and gold Sonics identity belongs to that history. OKC fans tell the move as their town earning a team, not borrowing a legacy.
insights.implication: Never use Sonics green or gold as a throwback. Start OKC heritage product in 2008.

insights.title: Oklahoma weather is the most ownable graphic language
insights.detail: The team name already comes from storms, and locals live with prairie wind, red dirt and huge sunset skies. All of it is more specific than a generic lightning bolt.
insights.implication: Use sky gradients, red clay tonal washes and wind-line patterns as signature textures instead of literal bolts.

insights.title: State pride outruns city pride
insights.detail: Thunder fandom reaches Tulsa and rural Oklahoma, where the identity is the state, not Oklahoma City alone. "Oklahoma" wordmarks fit that easily.
insights.implication: Offer statewide product beyond OKC-only tees: an Oklahoma wordmark, county and highway graphics.

retail-landscape.headline: The volume is at the mall. The taste is in a few small districts.
retail-landscape.summary: OKC is a driving town with no sneaker street. Volume sits at Penn Square, Quail Springs, OKC Outlets and the big-box chains, while Fanatics, Lids and the Paycom Center team store carry Thunder identity. Taste lives in the Plaza District, Paseo, Midtown and Automobile Alley, whose boutiques, vintage and Oklahoma-pride brands are where Nike earns credibility. Since the 2025 title, demand runs broad, not niche.

insights.title: Buyers come from the whole state
insights.detail: The Thunder are Oklahoma's only major-league team, so buyers come from Tulsa, Norman, Lawton, Stillwater, tribal-nation communities and rural towns, not just the metro. Online and big-box doors outsell any single neighborhood.
insights.implication: Plan assortment and allocation for the whole state. Tulsa and big-box doors get the volume Thunder product. OKC indie doors get the story pieces.

insights.title: Sooners and Cowboys share the closet
insights.detail: OU and OSU gear is daily wear, sold at Campus Corner in Norman and in Stillwater, where Eskimo Joe's is the famous t-shirt institution. Thunder apparel competes with crimson and orange for the same wallet.
insights.implication: Make Thunder City Edition and lifestyle product read as civic pride, not college-adjacent. Skip orange-heavy palettes that collide with OSU.

insights.title: Volume lives in malls and big-box stores
insights.detail: Families and teens buy shoes and jerseys at Penn Square Mall, Quail Springs Mall, the OKC Outlets (formerly Outlet Shoppes of Oklahoma City), Academy Sports, Dick's and Hibbett. Academy and Hibbett are especially strong in the state.
insights.implication: Win with core Nike basketball and Thunder jerseys at Academy, Dick's, Hibbett and Foot Locker. Treat them as the volume layer for every launch.

insights.title: Taste is set in a few small districts
insights.detail: Plaza District, Paseo, Midtown, Automobile Alley and Deep Deuce hold the local boutiques, vintage shops, makers, events and pop-ups. Their crowds are younger and more arts-minded than the arena's.
insights.implication: Seed City Edition and Nike Sportswear drops through collaborations and pop-ups in these districts. Credit and pay the local makers.

insights.title: No Nike community door in town
insights.detail: Nike's known owned presence is a Nike Factory Store at the outlet center, a volume and value door. OKC appears to have no Nike Well Collective or House of Hoops flagship.
insights.implication: Borrow venues to tell the community story: the arena, local courts, Plaza District pop-ups. Nike has no premium owned door here to host drops.

insights.title: Championship demand is broad
insights.detail: After the 2025 title and a seven-game West finals run in 2026, fans buy Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren jerseys and tees at every price tier. Casual, family and kid buyers outnumber collectors.
insights.implication: Stock deep in youth sizes and player-name apparel. Keep premium limited pieces for the few tastemaker doors.

retail-behavior.headline: Oklahoma stocks up on Thunder gear during August's tax-free weekend
retail-behavior.summary: The Thunder are effectively Oklahoma's only major-league team, so demand comes from the whole state, not just the metro. Shoppers watch their money and buy in person: malls, outlets, big-box stores, the arena. The 2025 title and back-to-back MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander are the emotional anchor. The calendar bends around an early-August school start, fall college football and spring playoffs in storm season.

insights.title: The early-August tax-free weekend
insights.detail: Oklahoma's annual sales tax holiday falls on the first full weekend of August and exempts clothing and footwear under $100 per item. It lands just as most Oklahoma districts start school, in the second week of August. Tees, shorts and shoes under $100 are the natural volume play.
insights.implication: Hold a clearly sub-$100 Thunder tier of tees, shorts, hoodies and kids' footwear. Have it in stores and on shelves by late July. $99 or lower is a real threshold here, not a nicety.

insights.title: Thunder fandom is a state identity
insights.detail: With no other major-league franchise in the state, Thunder fandom is a state identity. It stretches to Tulsa, Lawton, Norman, Stillwater and tribal communities, so drive-in trips to OKC malls and outlets matter as much as the Bricktown core.
insights.implication: Plan assortment and launches along the I-35, I-40 and Turner Turnpike corridors and in Tulsa retail, not only downtown OKC. Tulsa deserves its own pop-up or retail partner moment.

insights.title: Football takes the fall wallet
insights.detail: From September through Bedlam, OU crimson and OSU orange dominate Oklahoma closets and spending. The Thunder season tips off in late October, right into that overlap. Many Thunder fans are also Sooners or Cowboys fans.
insights.implication: Don't clash with college colorways in Oct-Nov. Lean on Thunder blue and sunset orange so nothing reads as a crimson or orange school knockoff. Time Thunder pushes to the NBA opener (Oct 20 at San Antonio) and Cup Nights.

insights.title: Fans buy like winners but check prices
insights.detail: After the 2025 title, a back-to-back MVP in Gilgeous-Alexander and a No. 1 West seed, Thunder fans buy like winners. The West finals loss to San Antonio keeps them hungry, not flat. Value-minded shoppers still check prices against knockoffs and Fanatics-style marketplaces.
insights.implication: Anchor on Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren names and numbers across a good-better-best ladder. Re-promote around playoff seeding in spring rather than over-buying early.

insights.title: Spring playoffs meet tornado season
insights.detail: April to June is both the NBA playoffs and Oklahoma's severe-weather peak. Fans watch at home or in bars, and storm days disrupt shopping. Summers run hot and long, fall is mild, and January-February can bring ice and wind.
insights.implication: Make playoff product lightweight and breathable: tees, shorts, mesh. Add layering pieces for fall arena nights and cold snaps. Push e-commerce and ship-to-store during storm weeks.

insights.title: Oklahomans shop in person
insights.detail: Oklahoma shoppers lean on malls (Penn Square, plus Utica Square and Woodland Hills in Tulsa), outlet centers, Academy Sports, Hibbett, Dick's, Lids and the arena store. Fanatics and Nike.com handle online. Sneaker drops exist but are smaller than coastal line culture.
insights.implication: Put volume in wide wholesale distribution and arena retail. Keep limited drops for a few credible local doors rather than building national-style line culture.

insights.title: Native nations run their own economy and calendar
insights.detail: Oklahoma is home to 39 federally recognized tribal nations. The Chickasaw, Choctaw and Cherokee, among others, run major businesses, casinos and community programs that drive local spending and sponsorships. Powwow and cultural calendars (Red Earth in June, tribal national holidays) run on their own timelines.
insights.implication: Work with Native designers and nation-run commerce directly, with credit, pay and approval. Never lift sacred or ceremonial imagery. Treat Native-created product as a partnership, not a theme.

factcheck.summary: The dossiers were mostly sound on team facts, which match the current facts (record, West finals loss, trades, Mara, Cup group, key dates). Three live checks found location errors: the outlet center is now OKC Outlets on I-40, Ma Der Lao Kitchen is in the Plaza District, and Shop Good is in Midtown. Other fixes cover the Hornets' 2005-07 history, Durant's titles, Collison's dates, Memphis's division, the banner night, the WCWS venue name and the Jones Assembly neighborhood. An invented SoSo slang term is gone. OKC didn't get Specter. The brief still needs work on Chanchaleune as Asian District anchor, Shop Good's placement, the 2026-27 vs 2027-28 City Edition framing, past-dated 2026 windows and the Oct 22 home status. Small businesses and 2027 event dates are queued as unverifiable.

issues.target: collection.name 'Red Earth, Open Sky' and calendar[11]
issues.problem: "Red Earth" is the name of the Red Earth Festival, the long-running Native arts festival the brief itself lists as a June community moment. "Red people" is also the Choctaw root of the state name. A Nike collection called Red Earth borrows a Native institution's name and invites a reading the brief never intended.
issues.fix: Rename the collection (for example "Red Clay, Open Sky" or "Clay & Sky"). Keep "Red Earth" only as a festival the team supports through paid, credited partners. Credit the Choctaw origin of "Oklahoma" in copy only if a Choctaw partner approves.

issues.problem: Statehood Day marks the 1907 dissolution of Indian Territory, and the re-push lands in Native American Heritage Month. The brief bans Land Run imagery, yet it sells a celebratory "Oklahoma" line on the anniversary of the same event, with no Native partner in the room.
issues.fix: Drop Statehood Day as a hook. Re-push the Oklahoma line on Cup Fridays or Thanksgiving week. Use November for a Native Heritage Month program built with a named nation and its artists, in a separate lane from the volume line.

issues.problem: Insight 0 says the market is Oklahoma, not OKC, and the volume line is an "Oklahoma" wordmark. Yet the City Edition is built around an original "Oklahoma City" script, with the state outline relegated to the jock tag. The flagship product contradicts the thesis.
issues.fix: Make the chest wordmark "Oklahoma" (Utah and Indiana set the precedent for state names), or put the state silhouette on the court apron and shorts. Get the NBA's early read on the wordmark in the design stage.

issues.problem: Insight 1 says blue is the one color a split Sooner-and-Cowboy household shares, and that browns and reds are risky. Yet the City Edition base is rust #A8442A, a non-blue jersey that sits between OU crimson, OSU orange and Texas burnt orange, with Thunder blue demoted to accent. The brief's own risk list flags the problem, then ships it.
issues.fix: Flip the hierarchy: Dark Blue or Thunder Blue body, with rust as horizon, yoke and number keyline. Or test the rust base in OKC and Tulsa fan panels against OU and OSU gear before committing. The jersey should still pass the blue-peace-treaty test.

issues.problem: Today is Oct 9. Plaza Walls and the State Fair (September) have already happened, so the Red Dirt preview is impossible. A launch the week of Oct 12 needs an NBA-licensed, tooled-and-dyed line for the new Storm-front gradient capsule and a Red Dirt capsule with a commissioned poster artist. That takes months, not days.
issues.fix: Say which items already exist in the Fall 2026 line, and re-skin only those for Oct 20. Move the Red Dirt capsule and the poster-artist commission to a Spring 2027 launch (April, with Festival of the Arts) and a September 2027 Plaza Walls preview.

issues.problem: 405 is the OKC metro area code. Tulsa is 918 and western Oklahoma is 580. A "405 state-outline hoodie" pushed hardest into Tulsa and small-town doors tells those buyers the product is for Oklahoma City. That undercuts the "one-team state" idea, and the culture dossier notes Tulsa as the in-state rival city.
issues.fix: Use the state outline alone for the statewide layer, and make 405 an OKC-metro tee. Add a 918 Tulsa tee and a 580 tee for the west and south, as a set, each aimed at a different door.

issues.target: partners, risks and opportunities[5], gym-pride (Tulsa and Booker T. Washington)
issues.problem: Tulsa is the second hub, with a Brookside pop-up and a Booker T. Washington gym program. Yet Greenwood, Black Wall Street and the 1921 massacre appear nowhere in the risks. The art dossier flags that memorial and Black Wall Street imagery belongs to local Black artists. A brand pop-up near that history, with no Tulsa-based Black partner named, is an avoidable error.
issues.fix: Add a risk line: no Greenwood, Black Wall Street or massacre imagery, and no launch dates near May 31 or Juneteenth, without a named Tulsa Black partner. Name a Tulsa-based partner for the Booker T. Washington gym program, and confirm what the school wants before any Thunder branding goes in.

issues.problem: The brief treats the First Americans Museum as a broker for a "nation-authored" edition. But the museum is a civic institution for 39 sovereign nations and can't speak for any of them. The brief names no nation, no Native artist working in apparel, and no pay structure beyond "credit and pay". Yatika Starr Fields is Cherokee, Osage and Muscogee, so one person could end up standing in for three nations.
issues.fix: Use the museum only for introductions, then go to the tribal commerce or cultural offices of the nations involved. Name the nation first, and set commission terms and approval rights in writing. Treat Fields as an individual artist with his own commission, not as a representative.

issues.target: calendar and missed signals (Native Heritage Month, Nike N7)
issues.problem: Oklahoma has 39 federally recognized nations and some of the biggest tribal-owned businesses in the market. Yet the brief has no November Native Heritage Month plan. It also ignores Nike's existing N7 program, the established, credentialed route for Indigenous-led product and giving. Nations that sponsor sports are the obvious statewide co-investor.
issues.fix: Add a November calendar slot that uses the N7 pathway and its Native design partners. Name an OKC-based nation or Native-owned designer as lead, and confirm the Thunder-side partners. Check which nations already hold Thunder sponsorships before approaching any.

issues.problem: Storm gradients, sunset skies and wind lines pass the swap test for Kansas City, Dallas or Denver, and the Thunder's own blue-orange-yellow palette is already a sunset. The brief also calls the gradient the signature texture without knowing whether a past City Edition or the 2008 identity used it. Its own verify list admits this.
issues.fix: Anchor the sky in something only Oklahoma has. Options: the Skydance Bridge sail line already in the brief, the flat sky-blue field of the state flag, or Tulsa and OKC Deco rooflines against a storm. Check the earlier Thunder City Editions before making the gradient a headline idea.

issues.problem: Pearl snaps, canvas, tooled leather and boot-cut denim also describe Fort Worth, Houston, Calgary and Cheyenne. Red Dirt music is as much a Texas scene as an Oklahoma one. The capsule aims at the Okie-pride crowd, but the brief cites no evidence that Thunder buyers want a Nike western line. It also barely addresses the NBA's growing Black and international fan base.
issues.fix: Cut to what is Oklahoma. Use Stillwater, Cain's Ballroom-style gig-poster lettering, Turnpike Troubadours or John Moreland shows booked by a Red Dirt venue, and Stockyards City stores like Langston's. Keep the capsule at priority 2. Pair it with a hoops-first line, so the Thunder don't read as a country team.

issues.problem: The Southside lowrider candy-paint release has a color (#4B3FA0) and a story, but no named partner, no car club or painter, no calendar moment and no month in the District Series rollout. It reads as a cue lifted from a community without a plan, the exact pattern the brief says it avoids.
issues.fix: Either name a Southside partner (a car club, painter or Capitol Hill business) and a community moment, such as Cinco de Mayo in Capitol Hill or Hispanic Heritage Month, or drop the release. Don't use candy-paint violet until a credited painter is attached.

issues.problem: The Asian District anchor is a chef (Jeff Chanchaleune), not a visual artist, and the brief says only "a Vietnamese or Lao OKC artist". Lunar New Year 2027 is Feb 6, four months out. That's too short for artist selection, contracts, NBA licensing sign-off and production. The brief also collapses the distinct events of the Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean and Lao communities.
issues.fix: Move the first release to Festival of the Arts or Paseo in spring 2027, and treat Lunar New Year 2028 as the Asian District date. Use the chef for introductions and a food pairing. Recruit the designer through the Asian District business association and Oklahoma Contemporary.

issues.target: opportunities[1] (Loud City playoff fast-turn) and retailPlaybook
issues.problem: The NBA and Fanatics typically control series-win and conference-round graphics, so a 48-hour turn into Academy, Dick's and Hibbett statewide is unrealistic for a Nike-led program. Ship-to-store for rural doors adds days. The Nike Factory Store carries overruns, not launch product.
issues.fix: Scope the fast-turn to Nike.com, the arena store and one or two metro doors, and coordinate graphics with the league's playoff licensing calendar. Take the Factory Store off the launch channels and use it to sell through the under-$100 line.

issues.problem: "Unfinished business" after a playoff loss fits the Spurs, Nuggets or any contender, and the copy asks fans to wear a loss. The brief's "earned, defiant champion details" is also unclear now that the Knicks are the reigning champions and the Thunder's title is from 2025.
issues.fix: Make the hook Thunder-specific: the Presti-built draft-and-develop core, the Mara and Williams development story, and "Loud City" at Paycom Center. Limit any 2025 champion reference to licensed commemorative marks.

issues.problem: The brief leads with an "SGA name-and-number tee" but ignores that SGA, a two-time MVP and Hamilton-born tunnel-fit regular, is a major style story. His shoe deal sits with Converse, a Nike-owned sister brand, so player product needs coordination. Name-and-number items also run through NBPA group licensing.
issues.fix: Add a tunnel-fit and Canadian-fan angle. Confirm which brand and licensing path covers SGA, Williams and Holmgren product. Keep the player tees to licensed formats Nike can actually ship.

issues.problem: The music dossier surfaces The Flaming Lips, OKC's psychedelic alt-rock institution, and the Red Dirt songwriters. But the partner list has no musician and no venue, apart from a passing Jones Assembly mention. Jabee is the only hip-hop voice.
issues.fix: Add one music partner on each side: a Red Dirt booker and an OKC hip-hop or alt-rock voice. Use their posters and stage lettering as the artist layer, so the gig-poster tee feels less like a design-team invention.

issues.problem: Okemah is a very small town hosting a folk festival. The calendar ties it to a shooting shirt and an Oklahoma wordmark tee, with no reason why festival-goers would buy either. It also invites use of Guthrie's catalog and name, which are separately rights-controlled.
issues.fix: Replace it with a real summer retail beat, such as the NBA Draft, Summer League or the August tax-free stock-in. Treat Guthrie as inspiration only unless the estate is licensed.

strengths: The "market is Oklahoma, not OKC" thesis is the brief's most specific idea. The Tulsa allocation, the small-town Academy and Hibbett doors and the August under-$100 tax holiday rest on real retail behavior no other NBA market shares.
The blue-led rule for split Sooner-and-Cowboy households is a sharp, usable design constraint with hex values. Outside the City Edition, the brief mostly respects it.
The avoid lists are strong: no Native regalia or Osage shield, no memorial, bombing or tornado-damage imagery, no Land Run or oil-derrick kitsch, no Sonics colors, no crimson-leaning reds.

Named partners (Plaza District Association, Jabee, Oklahoma Contemporary, Factory Obscura, Shop Good) are real, local and appropriate. The credit, pay and community-launch rule for every community-sourced piece is the right standard.

Palette hex values match the Thunder's published Dark Blue, Thunder Blue, Sunset and Yellow. The calendar correctly pins the Oct 20 San Antonio opener, the Oct 22 Denver game, Cup Fridays and Christmas at Minnesota.
critique.summary: A strong, locally grounded strategy whose statewide-value thesis is its best idea. But the flagship pieces undercut it. A rust-based "Oklahoma City" jersey contradicts the blue-peace-treaty, Oklahoma-not-OKC thesis, and the "Red Earth" name and the Statehood Day push risk real missteps with Native partners. Several September and mid-October launches are already past or unrealistic, the 405 tag misfires in Tulsa, and Tulsa's Greenwood history and Nike N7 are missing. Fix the naming, timing and Tulsa risks first. Confidence is medium: it rests on model knowledge, not a live check.
